title: Pauri 29, meaning: wisdom for food
hook: let wisdom be your food and compassion the one who serves it; the music sounds in every heart (Japji 29)

segments.voice: Yesterday, naad, the note in every heart, and your line, bhugat giaan: wisdom is the meal. Today, what the whole stanza means.

A school cook slips an extra scoop onto a tray because the kid in front of her looks like they've had a rough morning. A grandmother won't sit down until every plate is full. An uncle at a wedding keeps coming back with the tray. Years later, it can be the hands that stay in memory, more than the food. The same rice tastes different handed over by someone who wants you fed. In a gurdwara's langar, people sit in rows, and volunteers come down the line with a bucket and a ladle. Pauri 29 puts a server like that at the center of its meal.
screen: `THE EXTRA SCOOP.` → `THE HANDS STAY IN MEMORY.` → `THE LADLE IN LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak is speaking to yogis, in their own camp words. Their shared meal was bhugat, so he says: let wisdom be your bhugat. Not a rule, not a diet. What actually feeds you is understanding. Then he names the server: daiaa bhanddaaran, compassion is the keeper of the stores. Wisdom without compassion is a locked pantry: someone knows a great deal and hands none of it out, or hands it out with a sneer. In Pauri 29, wisdom is only a meal when compassion holds the ladle. Then the horn. The yogis blew a horn to sound the naad, the note they listened for in meditation. Nanak says: ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. It's already sounding, in every heart. No horn needed. The yogis honored their great teachers as Naths, masters. Nanak says the One is the true Nath, holding every creature on His string. And the miraculous powers some yogis worked for, riddhi and siddhi? Nanak calls them avaraa saad, other flavors. Tasty, maybe, but not the meal. Then a wide line: sanjog vijog, meeting and parting, both keep the world turning, and each of us receives our share as it is written. And the refrain, the yogis' own greeting turned toward God: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. So the menu is short. Wisdom to eat, compassion to serve it, and a note already playing in you.
screen: `WISDOM IS THE MEAL.` · `COMPASSION HOLDS THE LADLE.` · `THE NOTE IS ALREADY PLAYING.` · `POWERS ARE JUST OTHER FLAVORS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION SERVES THE FOOD.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one slow bite or sip; if not, picture your next meal. As you taste it, think of one thing you understand now that you didn't a year ago, and who handed it to you: a teacher, a parent, a friend, a stranger. Then rest, breathing, and listen for the note Nanak says is already sounding.
Nath, master, the yogis' name for their teacher. Wisdom as the meal, compassion as the one who serves it, a note in every heart, and miraculous powers called nothing more than other flavors.
Your line: compassion serves the food. Powers are side dishes; wisdom is the meal. Day two hundred twelve, done.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; in the gurdwara's langar, people still sit in rows and are served by volunteers with a ladle, which many hear as a living picture of compassion serving the meal.

what a scholar hears: every image answers a yogi practice: the camp meal, the horn's naad, the Nath masters, and the prized powers dismissed as avaraa saad.
